title: Blinking the Onboard LED
effect: The onboard LED stays on for 0.5 seconds and off for 0.5 seconds, repeating continuously.
technical: DDRB configures PB7 as an output, and the main loop changes its PORTB level with 500 ms delays using _delay_ms. This introduces register-level GPIO, bit operations, and building and running a minimal AVR C program.

title: Alternating Onboard and External LEDs
effect: The onboard LED turns on for 0.2 seconds and off for 0.2 seconds. An external yellow LED then follows the same pattern. The two LEDs repeat this sequence continuously.
technical: PB7 and PB4 are configured as outputs. Separate bit masks control the onboard and external LEDs, while 200 ms delays sequence their operation, demonstrating independent control of multiple pins on one port.

title: Setting LED Blink Counts and Intervals
effect: The LED blinks quickly three times, stays off for one second, then blinks slowly twice and remains off. Changing the blink counts and intervals produces different light sequences.
technical: The wait_ms and blink functions encapsulate delay and output logic. Count and interval parameters, const values, and fixed-width integer types organize the fast-blink, pause, and slow-blink sequence.

title: Cycling Through Three LED Colors
effect: Red, green, and blue LEDs light up in sequence, with a brief interval when all three are off between colors. The sequence repeats continuously. Changing the settings for each step changes the order and timing of the display.
technical: State arrays define the three LED outputs at each step, while a duration array defines 50 ms light intervals and 20 ms all-off intervals. A for loop indexes the arrays, separating output states from timing in a table-driven program.

title: Button-Controlled LED with a Reliable Input
effect: The LED lights while the button is held and turns off when it is released. The program continuously distinguishes pressing from releasing, with a clear released state even when the button is untouched.
technical: PB4 is configured as an input with an internal pull-up, making a press active-low. Reading PINB controls the PB5 output, combining input-direction configuration, pull-ups, and logical inversion to map button level to LED output.

title: Toggling an LED on Each Button Press
effect: One press turns the LED on; another turns it off. Holding the button does not repeatedly switch the light. This version does not yet filter the brief signal changes caused by mechanical contact bounce.
technical: The program retains the previous button reading, compares it with the current reading, and toggles the LED only on a falling edge. This distinguishes a sustained logic level from a discrete event; mechanical debouncing is not yet implemented.

title: Selecting Four LED Behaviors
effect: Successive presses select off, steady on, fast blinking, and slow blinking. Each blinking mode performs a short sequence and then leaves the LED off. The next press selects the following behavior.
technical: A mode variable increments on each falling edge and wraps to zero. A switch/case structure selects off, steady on, or blink sequences with different delays, implementing state-driven output control.

title: Displaying Button Bounce as LED Flashes
effect: After a button press, the program records how many times the button signal changes within a short interval. Once the button is released, the LED flashes that many times, showing the signal changes detected during a single press.
technical: A press starts a window of 100 samples spaced 50 microseconds apart. The program counts level transitions and displays the count through LED flashes after release, introducing mechanical-bounce sampling and event counting.

title: Reducing Duplicate Button Triggers
effect: The program waits for the button input to settle before accepting a change. The first accepted press lights the LED, and the next turns it off, reducing cases where one physical press is counted as several actions.
technical: Separate variables retain raw readings, candidate state, and confirmed state. A stability counter must reach its threshold before a transition is committed; confirmed events then toggle the LED, establishing incremental debouncing and edge-counting logic.

title: Different Light Responses to Short and Long Presses
effect: A short press followed by release makes the LED flash quickly three times. Holding the button longer before releasing it produces five slow flashes. One button therefore selects two different light responses.
technical: The program accumulates press duration after debouncing and selects a fast- or slow-blink function on release using a threshold. Button lifecycle handling, timing decisions, and output actions are kept separate.

title: Controlling Two LEDs with Two Buttons
effect: Each button controls its own LED. The two lights retain their individual states, so the buttons can be operated in turn and the LEDs can remain in different on/off combinations.
technical: Each input has independent debounce counters, confirmed states, and press counts. These control PB6 and PB7 separately, extending single-input state handling without interference from shared variables.

title: Viewing Button Events and Counts on a Computer
effect: The computer displays a startup message when the board begins running. Operating either button displays its event and total press count, while both LEDs remain controllable.
technical: USART0 is configured for transmission at the selected baud rate. Startup messages, button events, and counts are encoded as ASCII, combining GPIO control with serial debugging and integer-to-decimal text conversion.

title: Controlling Two LEDs with Computer Commands
effect: Typing on_1, off_1, on_2, or off_2 switches the two LEDs independently. The status command reports their current states, and help lists the commands. The program also handles backspace and reports commands that are too long or unrecognized.
technical: A bounded character buffer receives UART commands and handles backspace, line endings, and excess input. String comparisons dispatch LED control and status requests, forming a basic command parser.

title: Switching a Buzzer with Computer Commands
effect: Sending on from the computer makes the buzzer sound; sending off stops it. Entered text is echoed back, and an error message appears if the command is too long.
technical: UART line reception and length checking are reused to recognize on/off commands, set the buzzer pin level, and echo the input. This maps text commands to an active-buzzer output.

title: Detecting Button Changes While an LED Blinks
effect: The LED changes between on and off about once per second. Pressing or releasing the button during blinking still produces a change message on the computer, without waiting for a complete light sequence to finish.
technical: The main loop alternates timing updates, periodic LED checks, and button debouncing. Elapsed-time comparisons update outputs and emit state events instead of blocking for an entire blink sequence, creating a cooperative task structure.

title: Timing an LED with a Hardware Timer
effect: The LED repeats a pattern of roughly one second on and one second off. Switching follows the time continuously recorded by the development board.
technical: Timer1 operates in CTC mode, with its prescaler and OCR1A configured for a 1 ms compare-match interrupt. The ISR updates system_ms, and the main loop atomically reads a time snapshot to schedule the LED.

title: Continuously Reporting System Uptime
effect: The LED changes state once per second while the computer repeatedly displays SYSTEM ALIVE and the elapsed time in milliseconds. The increasing time helps show whether the program is still running and whether its numeric output is correct.
technical: An ISR updates a volatile uint32_t millisecond counter. ATOMIC_BLOCK provides a consistent snapshot for decimal-text output, addressing interrupt-shared data, multibyte atomicity, and numeric type width.

title: Running LED, Button, and Reporting Tasks Together
effect: The LED changes state every 0.5 seconds, while button presses accumulate in a counter. About every two seconds, the computer reports the current time, LED state, and button count. These functions continue while the button is being used.
technical: A shared 1 ms tick supports separate timestamps for the LED, serial reports, and button debouncing. Tasks run cooperatively at different periods, using uint32_t counters and serial status output to observe execution.

title: Generating Stepper Pulses and Direction Changes
effect: The board continuously sends motor-control signals and changes the direction setting about every five seconds. The computer receives a running message about every four seconds. The signals can also be measured without connecting a motor.
technical: Timer1 output compare generates STEP pulses, while Timer3 maintains the system timebase. The main loop schedules DIR changes and reports independently, allowing hardware pulse generation and periodic software tasks to proceed together.

title: First Stepper Motor Operation
effect: A stepper motor is connected through a driver and a separate power supply so it can turn in response to the board's signals. Changing the direction signal allows its rotation to be observed in the opposite direction. This hardware exercise reuses Project 19.
technical: The original exercise connects STEP/DIR signals to an external current-limiting driver and checks phase current, separate power, and common ground. It connects logic-level control to a physical stepper drive using the Project 19 workspace.
note: Hardware exercise: reuses Project 19; the repository has no separate Project 20 directory.

title: Receiving Commands During Motor Operation
effect: Computer commands can start or stop the motor, adjust its speed, reverse direction, and request its status. New commands are still received while the motor is running. Periodic reports show speed, direction, and whether the motor is running.
technical: Hardware maintains STEP output while the main loop incrementally receives commands in a persistent character buffer. Motor interfaces handle start/stop, speed, and direction, with periodic status reports, so command reception does not block motion control.

title: Stepper Acceleration, Deceleration, and an Automatic Demo
effect: The motor gradually accelerates to its selected speed and slows down when stopping. The computer can change speed and acceleration and display phase changes and speed logs. An automatic demo accelerates, runs for a set interval, and decelerates to a stop.
technical: A motion state machine updates the step-frequency ramp over time and distinguishes acceleration, cruise, and deceleration. A demo task uses state transitions and timing to request a stop, while logs record speed and phase changes.

title: Comparing Motor Smoothness, Load, and Heating
effect: This experiment compares motor smoothness, sound, and heating under different driver settings and loads. The experiment log should record speed, load, temperature, and any missed steps so the settings can be compared.
technical: The original exercise varies microstepping, current, and load and records speed, temperature rise, and missed steps to compare smoothness and load capacity. The repository does not contain a separate experiment project.
note: Hardware exercise from the original project plan; the repository has no separate Project 23 directory.

title: Stepper Homing, Limits, and Emergency Stop
effect: The motor can find its starting position, back away after reaching a switch, and approach again slowly to establish a reference. Reaching a limit switch or pressing the emergency stop stops motion and produces a status report. Switch problems or failure to find the starting reference also produce fault reports.
technical: Limit checking, ESTOP, and homing are separate modules. Interrupt-level guard checks stop pulses, while a homing state machine handles search, backoff, slow approach, and timeout, establishing fault states and exception paths.

title: Positioning and Repeated Round Trips
effect: Once the motor has found its starting reference, a computer command can send it to a specified position. Two points and a repeat count can also define a round-trip task. Motion status, configuration, and logs remain available while stop, limit, and emergency-stop inputs are handled. Long help messages are sent in portions so reporting does not hold up other work.
technical: Positioning, repeat, homing, and safety tasks organize motion. The reporting module retains pending requests and sends output according to free TX-buffer space, preventing long messages from blocking the main loop and deceleration updates.

title: Receiving Ammonia Sensor Data and Reporting Its Status
effect: The computer shows incoming raw data, concentration readings, and states such as warming up, valid, or out of date. Invalid or incomplete data is counted as an error. Older readings are identified as such, while sensor reception and motion tasks continue separately.
technical: A dedicated UART validates frame headers, length, checksum, and fields before committing a complete concentration value. Reception and protocol adaptation are separated, with sample-age and warm-up tracking. ZE03 is the current default; ZE801 support awaits protocol confirmation.

title: Fixed Brightness and a Fading LED
effect: The LED can be switched off, held at a selected brightness, or made to fade repeatedly up and down. The computer can adjust the fading cycle and report the current brightness and mode. Motor and serial tasks continue during the light effect.
technical: Timer4 hardware PWM maintains the output, while an LED task updates duty cycle from system time. Fixed brightness and an adjustable fading period separate carrier generation from brightness-envelope updates.

title: Knob-Controlled Brightness and Voltage Readout
effect: In knob-control mode, turning the knob changes LED brightness. The computer can show the raw reading, calculated voltage, update time, and corresponding brightness so the changes can be observed together.
technical: Periodic potentiometer ADC samples are converted to millivolts using the reference voltage and mapped to PWM duty cycle. Timestamps and validity flags separate acquisition, data state, and dimming output.

title: Reading Two Inputs and Selecting the Dimming Source
effect: The computer shows readings, voltages, and update times for two inputs and lets the user choose which one controls LED brightness. After switching sources, the LED follows the newly selected input while readings from the other channel are retained.
technical: A shared ADC scans channels through the MUX and stores independent sample snapshots. The dimming module selects its source and checks channel validity, extending acquisition to multiple inputs.

title: Smoothing and Calibrating Knob Readings
effect: The computer can compare raw readings, averages, calibrated values, and the resulting brightness. Smoothing strength, the threshold for brightness changes, and the knob's usable endpoints can be adjusted to observe how much flicker is reduced and whether the response becomes slower.
technical: Each input maintains a moving-average window, calibration endpoints, and a hysteresis threshold. Calibration and mapping update a held brightness value, allowing filter stability to be compared with step-response delay.

title: Automatic LED Control from Ambient Light
effect: In automatic mode, the light turns on as the surroundings become dark and turns off as they brighten. Different turn-on and turn-off conditions reduce repeated switching near the boundary. The computer also shows light readings, settings, and the number of switches.
technical: Averaged and normalized light-sensor readings drive hysteresis control with separate on/off thresholds. Polarity and data freshness are checked before applying the input to a nonblocking automatic-lighting task.

title: Playing Tones, a Scale, and a Melody
effect: Computer commands can play a tone at a selected pitch and duration, a complete scale, or a preset short melody, and can stop playback early. Other tasks remain active during playback. Status reports show the current note, frequency, and remaining time.
technical: A timer generates the requested square-wave frequency, while a PROGMEM note table stores frequencies and durations. A playback state machine schedules notes, rests, and gaps independently of waveform generation.

title: Counting External Events and Comparing Detection Methods
effect: The computer displays event counts from two detection methods, their rates per second, and the difference between the counts. Button mode separately counts accepted presses. Faster input signals can reveal missed events. Counting can be started, stopped, or cleared.
technical: INT5 and main-loop polling count events on the same input, with periodic rate and count-difference calculations. Button mode adds debouncing, and atomic snapshots support comparison of interrupt edge capture with polling.

title: Ultrasonic Distance Measurement and Proximity Alerts
effect: The computer shows distance, the latest measurement time, and measurement status. Raw, mean-filtered, and median-filtered distances can be compared. A message appears when an object enters the selected proximity range. Missing echoes, timeouts, and abnormal signals produce distinct status reports.
technical: A state machine triggers measurements, waits for rising and falling echo edges, measures pulse width, and converts it to distance. Timeouts, mean/median filters, and hysteretic alerts distinguish measurement errors from valid distance changes.

title: Scanning Connected Device Addresses
effect: The computer lists devices that respond on the shared connection, identified by their addresses. It also shows scan progress, device count, and elapsed time. A scan can be canceled. Statistics and error messages identify missing responses, timeouts, and connection faults.
technical: An I2C state machine probes 7-bit addresses and records ACK/NACK responses. START, address, and STOP transactions proceed incrementally, with timeout, bus-error, cancellation, and retry tracking.

title: MPU-6050 Identification and Three-Axis Acceleration
effect: The computer shows the sensor's identity and acceleration readings along the X, Y, and Z axes. Single readings or continuous sampling are available, with an indication of whether data is still fresh. Failed reads retain the previous complete sample and its age while recovery is attempted. Repeated failures eventually stop retries and produce a report.
technical: MPU-6050 identity checks, reset, configuration readback, and three-axis sampling run in sequence, committing only complete results. Recovery uses bounded retries and backoff; only a valid sample clears the consecutive-failure counter.

title: SPI Data Verification and Voltage Output
effect: The computer can start multiple send/receive tests, compare transmitted data with returned data, and show passes, mismatches, or errors. With an MCP4921 voltage-output module connected, it can send a target value and report the last value sent and its theoretical voltage. Tests and voltage commands share the communication interface in a coordinated order.
technical: The SPI loopback task sends test patterns in chunks and checks them byte by byte. A DAC task sends MCP4921 control words, with bus ownership coordinating access. Loopback verification, completed transmission, and measured analog output remain distinct.

title: A Multi-Page OLED Status Display
effect: The small display switches among motion, sensor, and system pages. These show motor position and speed, distance and acceleration readings, counts, and communication states. Emergency stops, limits, stale data, and device failures produce notices. The display updates changed content, and communication failures produce retry messages on the computer.
technical: The SSD1306 interface renders state snapshots into a framebuffer row by row. Dirty-region tracking and incremental I2C transfers support partial refreshes, while bounded retries with backoff handle faults and limit display workload.

title: Servo Angle, Speed, and Knob Tracking
effect: Computer commands set a servo's target angle and turning speed, or make its target follow a selected knob input. The commanded angle changes gradually. An emergency stop or invalid knob data stops control pulses and reports the reason; a new command is needed to resume.
technical: Angles map to servo pulse widths, with rate-limited command updates at fixed time steps. ESTOP and ADC data age are checked before output; faults stop pulses. Target angle, commanded output, and actual position feedback are explicitly distinguished.

title: Automatic Round Trips and Integrated System Control
effect: After the motor finds its starting reference, the user sets positions A and B and a cycle count from the computer. The motor first moves to A, then completes the requested A-to-B-to-A cycles and finishes at A. Reports show the current phase, completed cycles, target, and position tracked by step count, and record how the run ended. Completion, manual stops, and faults have distinct outcomes. The system coordinates manual commands with automatic movement and prevents changes to the plan during a run. Sensors, the display, and other modules continue operating while the system summarizes their states.
technical: A system state machine coordinates homing, plan setup, positioning, and automatic round trips. Task arbitration constrains manual/automatic operations, and runlog records progress and termination reasons. Peripheral tasks advance independently, with system-level state aggregation.
